results.title: 5. Machine Learning Fundamentals
results.content: Machine learning algorithms build a model based on sample data, known as "training data", in order to make predictions or decisions without being explicitly programmed to do so. Instead of having to write the rules that makes up a particular application, we can feed data and results(or labels) to the machine learning model, and its job can be to determine the set of rules that map the data and labels. Labeling data is one of the most challenging things in machine learning. Your job as machine learning engineer is to find the relevant data that you can use to solve the presented problem. What makes machine learning different to normal software development is that it involves data and codes(model). Data is the primary ingredient of machine learning, and better models are the results of better data. Building a machine learning model that can fit the training data well is not a trivial task.

results.title: Ilia Ekhlakov's Post
results.content: • Fast, strong baseline for multi-class problems • Probabilities are often well-calibrated • Interpretable: each weight shows feature → class association • Works well with high-dim, sparse inputs (text, one-hot, hashing) How it learns • Fits K weight vectors jointly (true multinomial); shared denominator makes classes compete • One-vs-rest is similar only when classes are well-separated; joint training usually better Quick knobs • penalty: L2 (default), L1 (sparse), or elastic-net • C (or lambda): inverse regularization strength (smaller → more regularization) • solver: lbfgs / saga (saga supports L1 and large+sparse) • class\_weight='balanced' for skewed data • max\_iter: increase if “didn’t converge” • multi\_class='multinomial' (preferred) vs 'ovr' Watch outs • Feature scaling: standardize numeric features; keep sparse one-hots as is • Collinearity: correlated features inflate weights → use regularization • Imbalance: can collapse to majority class → class\_weight, resampling, or focal loss (if supported) • Nonlinearity: linear model; add interactions/buckets or use trees/NNs for complex boundaries • Leakage: no future info; for time data, split by time Evaluation • Macro-F1 (treat classes equally) and Weighted-F1 (respect prevalence) • Top-k accuracy (if users see multiple suggestions) • AUROC/PR per class (ovr) for deeper insight • Expected calibration error (ECE) if acting on probabilities Real-time example: Virat Kohli—next-ball outcome prediction Goal: predict the next delivery outcome when Virat Kohli is on strike.
